lessons.title: Cap Rate and Price-to-Rent Ratio: Quick Tests for Any Property

children.text: You now know how to calculate gross yield, net yield, appreciation and total return. But when a broker sends you five listings on a Saturday morning, you do not have time to build a ten-year model for each one. Professional property investors use two quick tests to decide which listings deserve that time: the cap rate and the price-to-rent ratio. Used together, they tell you in minutes whether a property is priced on its income, priced on hope, or dangerously sensitive to a change in interest rates. By the end of this lesson you will be able to run a five-minute screen on any Indian property and reverse-engineer the growth assumption hidden inside its price.

body.text: A property's cap rate tells you what the market assumes about its future. A low cap rate means buyers expect strong growth; a high one means they expect little. Your job is to decide whether that assumption is believable.

children.text: What a Cap Rate Is

markDefs.definition: Capitalisation rate: a property's net operating income divided by its current market value. It measures the income return a buyer gets at today's price, ignoring loans and tax.
Net operating income based on a normal, sustainable year, including a realistic allowance for vacancy rather than a best-case fully let year.

children.text: The
cap rate

is net operating income divided by market value. It looks almost identical to the net yield from Chapter 2, and the arithmetic is the same. The difference is purpose. Net yield answers "what does my purchase earn?" and uses your all-in cost. Cap rate answers "what is this property worth, and how does it compare with others?" and uses today's market value with a
stabilised NOI

body.latex: \text{Cap Rate} = \frac{\text{Stabilised NOI}}{\text{Market Value}} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \text{Market Value} = \frac{\text{Stabilised NOI}}{\text{Cap Rate}}
body.caption: The same formula read two ways: as a return, or as a valuation.

body.title: Complete the formula
body.textWithBlank: Cap rate = stabilised net operating income ÷ current market ___.
body.explanation: Cap rate uses today's market value, not what you originally paid. That is what makes it useful for valuing and comparing properties.

children.text: Cap Rates as a Valuation Tool

markDefs.definition: A fall in the cap rate buyers accept, which pushes values up even if income is unchanged.
A rise in the cap rate buyers demand, which pushes values down even if income is unchanged.

children.text: Flip the formula and cap rates become a pricing tool. Commercial valuers and REIT managers value income-producing property this way. Because the cap rate sits in the denominator, small changes move values a lot. When buyers accept a lower cap rate, called
cap rate compression
, values rise. When they demand a higher one, called
cap rate expansion
, values fall, even though not a rupee of rent has changed.

body.title: Value of a Property Earning ₹10 Lakh NOI at Different Cap Rates (₹ lakh)

body.latex: \text{Change in Value (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Old Cap Rate}}{\text{New Cap Rate}} - 1\right) \times 100
body.caption: With NOI unchanged. A move from 5% to 6% cuts value by 16.7%; a move from 8% to 9% cuts it by only 11.1%.

body.text: Low cap rates are fragile. The same 1 percentage point rise wipes out a much larger share of value when the starting cap rate is low. That is why low-yield property behaves like a long-dated bond: very sensitive to changes in interest rates and in what buyers expect.

body.title: Value a pre-leased shop
body.prompt: A pre-leased shop in Chandigarh earns a stabilised NOI of ₹7.2 lakh a year. Similar pre-leased shops in the area trade at a 6% cap rate. What is the shop worth, in crore?
body.explanation: Market value = ₹7,20,000 ÷ 0.06 = ₹1,20,00,000, or ₹1.2 crore. If the seller is asking ₹1.5 crore, the implied cap rate is ₹7.2 lakh ÷ ₹1.5 crore = 4.8%, well below comparable shops, and the buyer would need a good reason to pay that premium.

children.text: The Growth Assumption Hidden in Every Cap Rate

markDefs.definition: The minimum total annual return an investor wants from an asset, given its risk and the returns available elsewhere.

children.text: This is the most useful idea in the lesson. Total return is income plus growth. If an investor has a
required return
and the property's income grows steadily, the cap rate is roughly what is left after subtracting expected growth. Rearrange it and any cap rate reveals the growth a buyer must be assuming.

body.latex: \text{Cap Rate} \approx r - g \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad g \approx r - \text{Cap Rate}
body.caption: r = required annual return, g = expected annual growth in NOI and value, assumed steady over a long period.

children.text: This one line explains the whole course. A residential flat at a 2.5% cap rate, bought by someone who wants 10% a year, only makes sense if its income and value grow about 7.5% a year, every year. An office at a 7.5% cap rate needs only about 2.5% growth to deliver the same 10%. Residential property is cheap on income and expensive on hope. Commercial property is the reverse.

body.title: Where cap rate ≈ r − g comes from

children.text: If a property pays NOI next year that then grows at a constant rate g forever, and investors discount future income at a required return r, the value of all that future income is a growing perpetuity. It is the same logic used to value stocks with steadily growing dividends.

content.caption: NOI divided by value is the cap rate. The relationship is an approximation: real properties do not grow at a constant rate forever.

children.text: Use it as a reasonableness check, not a precise forecast. Its power is in exposing assumptions: when the growth it implies is far above what incomes, rents and inflation can plausibly deliver, the price is resting on hope.

body.title: Reverse-engineer the growth
body.prompt: A luxury flat in South Mumbai trades at a 3.5% cap rate. A buyer wants a 12% total annual return. Roughly what annual growth in rent and value is the buyer assuming?
body.explanation: g ≈ r − cap rate = 12% − 3.5% = 8.5% a year, sustained for a long time. Ask whether rents and prices in that locality can realistically grow that fast for decades. If you believe 5% is more realistic, the flat is priced to deliver about 8.5% a year to you, not 12%.

children.text: The Price-to-Rent Ratio, Revisited
In Chapter 1 you met the price-to-rent ratio as the flip side of gross yield. It needs no cost estimates, which makes it the fastest test of all, and it is especially useful in three ways.
Comparing neighbours.
If most flats in a society trade at 28 times rent and one is listed at 36 times, it is either overpriced or under-rented. Find out which.
Tracking a market over time.
A locality's ratio rising from 25 to 35 over a few years means prices are running ahead of rents. Appreciation is increasingly resting on expectations rather than rental demand.
Buy vs rent decisions.

A high ratio means renting the same home is cheap relative to owning it. You will often see rules of thumb from overseas markets that treat anything above 20 as expensive, but most Indian metro flats sit well above that, so compare within Indian localities rather than against foreign benchmarks.

columns.label: Price-to-rent ratio
points: Uses gross rent: needs no cost estimates
Fastest possible screen, even from a listing
Ideal for comparing similar flats in one locality
Misleading across property types with very different costs

columns.label: Cap rate
points: Uses net operating income after vacancy and costs
Needs a few minutes of cost estimates
Fair across flats, offices, shops and warehouses
Directly reveals implied growth and interest rate sensitivity

children.text: The Five-Minute Screen: A Kolkata Example

markDefs.definition: The difference between a property's cap rate and a benchmark such as the 10-year government bond yield. It shows how much extra income you earn for taking property risk.

children.text: Here are two listings in Kolkata: a pre-leased office unit in Salt Lake Sector V for ₹1.8 crore, and a 2BHK flat in New Town for ₹75 lakh. Stabilised NOI already allows for a month of vacancy and the owner's running costs. The screen also uses the
spread
over a 10-year government bond yield, assumed at 6.4%, and a required return of 10%.

body.caption: Five-minute screen on two Kolkata listings (illustrative)
headers: Office unit, Salt Lake Sector V

cells: 5. Implied growth at a 10% required return
6. Value change if cap rate rises 1 point

children.text: The office's cap rate barely beats a government bond, so it is not cheap for its risk, but its implied growth of about 3.6% is modest and believable. The flat pays far less than a government bond and needs about 7.3% a year of growth to earn 10%. Neither is automatically a buy or a pass. The screen tells you exactly what you would have to believe for each one to work, and which listing deserves a full analysis.

body.text: Residential prices in India are not set by cap rates day to day. Most buyers are families purchasing homes to live in, and they do not price flats as income streams. So a 1 point rise in cap rates will not automatically cut flat prices by a quarter. But the arithmetic still shows the underlying fragility: a low-yield flat has almost no income cushion if growth expectations fade.

body.title: Read the compression
body.question: Over three years, the NOI of a pre-leased warehouse stays at ₹20 lakh a year, but the cap rate buyers accept for similar warehouses falls from 8% to 7%. What happened to its value?
options: It stayed the same, because NOI did not change
body.explanation: Value moved from ₹20 lakh ÷ 0.08 = ₹2.5 crore to ₹20 lakh ÷ 0.07 = ₹2.857 crore, a rise of 8 ÷ 7 − 1 = 14.3%. This is cap rate compression: the owner gained over ₹35 lakh without the rent changing at all. It can reverse just as easily.

body.title: Screen a GIFT City listing
body.scenario: Sunita Reddy, a 50-year-old chartered accountant in Ahmedabad, is offered a pre-leased office unit in GIFT City for ₹1.2 crore. It rents for ₹85,000 a month. Sunita estimates ₹1.5 lakh a year in owner's costs, including a vacancy allowance. The 10-year government bond yields about 6.4%, and Sunita wants an 11% total annual return from any property investment.
body.prompt: Run the five-minute screen: gross yield, price-to-rent ratio, cap rate, spread over the bond yield, implied growth, and the value change if the cap rate rises by 1 percentage point. What does the screen tell Sunita?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Gross yield: ₹85,000 × 12 = ₹10,20,000. ₹10,20,000 ÷ ₹1,20,00,000 = 8.5%.
2. Price-to-rent ratio: ₹1.2 crore ÷ ₹10.2 lakh = 11.8.
3. Stabilised NOI: ₹10,20,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹8,70,000. Cap rate: ₹8,70,000 ÷ ₹1,20,00,000 = 7.25%.
4. Spread over the bond: 7.25% − 6.4% = 0.85 percentage points of extra income for taking on property risk, single-tenant risk and illiquidity.
5. Implied growth: 11% − 7.25% = about 3.75% a year. Achievable if rents rise roughly with inflation.
6. Rate shock: at an 8.25% cap rate, value = ₹8,70,000 ÷ 0.0825 = about ₹1.05 crore, a fall of about 12.1%.
7. Conclusion: the price rests mostly on income, not hope, which suits Sunita's 11% target. The thin spread over government bonds means the key questions are tenant quality, remaining lock-in, whether the rent is at market level, and how quickly a vacant unit in GIFT City re-lets. It passes the screen and deserves a full analysis, not an automatic yes.

body.title: The five-minute property screen
steps: Calculate gross yield from signed rent and asking price.
Calculate the price-to-rent ratio and compare it with similar properties nearby.
Estimate stabilised NOI with a vacancy allowance and owner's costs, then calculate the cap rate.
Compare the cap rate with the 10-year government bond yield to see the spread.
Subtract the cap rate from your required return to find the growth you must believe in.
Recalculate value at a cap rate 1 percentage point higher to test sensitivity.
Only build a full cash flow model for listings where the implied assumptions look believable.

cards.definition: Stabilised NOI divided by current market value.
Net operating income in a normal year, including a realistic vacancy allowance.
A fall in cap rates that raises values with no change in income.
A rise in cap rates that lowers values with no change in income.
The cap rate roughly equals required return minus expected growth, so growth ≈ required return minus cap rate.
The cap rate minus a benchmark such as the 10-year government bond yield.
Price divided by annual gross rent. Best for comparing similar properties in the same area.

points: Cap rate = stabilised NOI ÷ current market value; flip it and value = NOI ÷ cap rate.
Net yield judges your own purchase using all-in cost; cap rate values and compares properties using market value.
Cap rate compression raises values and expansion lowers them, even when rent does not change.
Low cap rates are fragile: a 1 point rise cuts value far more from 3% than from 7%.
Growth implied by a price ≈ required return − cap rate. Residential flats often imply 7% or more a year; offices far less.
The price-to-rent ratio is the fastest screen for similar properties in one locality; the cap rate is fairer across property types.
Use quick tests to decide which listings deserve a full analysis, not to make the final decision.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The people, properties, rents, costs, bond yield and required returns shown are illustrative assumptions. Check current government bond yields and actual rents and costs before analysing a real property, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making any decision.
